title: Japanese military "comfort women" system
summary: After the First Shanghai Incident in 1932, the first "comfort station" was set up in Shanghai for a Japanese naval brigade; stations multiplied after the Sino-Japanese war began in 1937, wherever the military went. A 1998 UN report quoted by the Asian Women’s Fund dates the system from 1932 to the end of the Second World War. The Fund lists researchers’ estimates of 20,000 to 410,000 women and says no survey has fixed a total.

uncertainty.note: Start: the first station in Shanghai in 1932 (Asian Women’s Fund, NAHF). End: the Fund quotes a 1998 UN report giving “Between 1932 and the end of the Second World War”; 1945 is that war’s end.

where.historical_name: Shanghai, Republic of China (site of the first comfort station for a Japanese naval brigade)

importance.justification: A military-run system of sexual slavery across the Asia-Pacific war; its later exposure became a major redress and diplomatic issue.

audience_note: Concerns wartime sexual slavery and mass sexual violence; stated in general terms without detail. Estimates of the number of women vary widely and are attributed, not settled.

related.because: Kim Hak-sun's 1991 public testimony was the first by a survivor in South Korea about this system.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the end year (not on opened pages) and of the estimate range, which is the Asian Women's Fund's own list of researchers (Hata 1999: 20,000; Su Zhiliang 1999: 410,000; Yoshimi 1995: 45,000-200,000). The AWF is Japanese-government-linked and is party to the debate; a scholarly source should confirm. Pin is Shanghai, the site of the first station, not the whole system.
